verses.translation_literal: Of Solomon. O God, your judgments to the king give, and your righteousness to the king's son.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song for Solomon, the young king, and it begins on its knees. O God, put your own justice into the king's hands. Put your own righteousness into the son of a king.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a prayer, not a boast: the opening word is an imperative, 'give!', addressed to God over a throne that has just changed hands. In the ancient Near East a king was the supreme judge, and Egyptian and Mesopotamian kings claimed their justice from the sun-god Shamash or from Maat. Israel's psalmist insists that royal justice is borrowed; the king has none of his own, and it is God's 'judgments' (mishpatim) he must be given.

The KJV makes 'A Psalm for Solomon' a separate line (72:0). In Hebrew it is one breath: lishlomoh, 'Of / for / concerning Solomon', with the lamed deliberately open, so the tradition can read the psalm as written by Solomon, for him, or about the ideal king he stands for. 'King' and 'son of the king' are a parallel pair for one person: the reigning king who is also a royal heir, which makes this a dynastic prayer. The KJV 'thy judgments' is accurate but reads as 'laws'; here it means the capacity to decide rightly. Do not play the actor as demanding. He asks, and he asks for what he cannot make himself.

philological_notes.note: The prefixed lamed can mean 'of' (authorship), 'for' (dedication) or 'about'. Ibn Ezra explains it here as meaning 'on behalf of'. Rashi and Radak take Solomon as the object of David's prayer.

Plural 'judgments': decisions and the right to decide. The king is asked to receive God's own verdicts as his own. Malbim distinguishes mishpat (justice between people) from tzedaqah (right action before God).
'Your righteousness': God's own rightness of dealing, which makes verdicts reliable. Radak glosses it 'your straightness'.

verses.translation_literal: He will judge your people with righteousness, and your poor with judgment.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let him judge your people with righteousness, and your afflicted ones, the poor, with true judgment.
verses.directors_commentary:
The prayer turns into a portrait. 'Your people... your poor': the king is a steward, and both groups still belong to God. The pairing is deliberate. Tzedek (right order) is for 'the people'; mishpat (the proper verdict) is for 'the poor' -- the 'aniyyim, those with no strong family or patron to speak for them in the gate. In a world where judges were often bribed or leaned toward the powerful, the test of a king was whether a poor man's case was heard as carefully as a rich man's.

The KJV 'with judgment' for mishpat is a trap: in modern English 'judgment' sounds like condemnation. The Hebrew means a fair hearing and a right decision. ASV 'justice' is closer. The verb is yadin, from din, a rarer word for 'judge' than shaphat, and it signals a judge's active deciding. Hebrew grammar allows both a wish and a promise here; the actor can play it either as hope or as certainty.

philological_notes.note: 'Your poor': from the root of affliction, one made low. Ibn Ezra reads it as including the poor whom the powerful, even rich ones, press down. 'Your' marks them as God's own clients.

A verdict according to law. Malbim says the poor are judged strictly by the Torah, while the people at large are judged also by equity. Metzudat David: he does not favour the rich party against the poor.

verses.translation_literal: Mountains will carry peace to the people, and hills, in righteousness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the mountains themselves will carry peace down to the people, and the hills will carry it too, because the land is righteous.
verses.directors_commentary:
A startling picture: the highlands, where Israel's fields and terraces were hardest to farm, become porters bearing peace on their shoulders. The verb nasa' is 'lift, carry', the same verb used for carrying a load or a gift. The point is that justice in the gate shows up in the fields. Rashi and Metzudat David see the hills yielding harvest, so that nobody is envious of his neighbour; Rashi cites Zech 3:10, 'each man under his vine'. In a rain-fed country where the hill-country harvest decided who ate, peace and plenty were one idea: shalom.

The KJV 'little hills' adds 'little'; Hebrew has just geva'ot, hills, as the poetic partner of harim, mountains. The final phrase 'in righteousness' hangs between the two lines: either the hills carry peace by righteousness, or they carry righteousness. BBE's 'the hills righteousness' takes the second, a stretch. Ibn Ezra offers two readings, 'because of righteousness', or 'righteousness' as a synonym of peace. Keep the grammar open.

philological_notes.note: 'They will carry/lift'. The mountains are the subject. Rashi ties the peace carried to the abundance mountains yield; Malbim to the harvest in the hills that removes the motive for quarrel.
'In/by righteousness'. The preposition can mean 'by means of', 'because of', or be a simple adverbial. Ibn Ezra weighs these.

verses.translation_literal: He will judge the afflicted of [the] people; he will save the sons of [the] needy; and he will crush [the] oppressor.
verses.translation_dramatic: He will take up the case of the afflicted among the people, and the weakest of the needy will find in him a rescuer. And the one who squeezes and robs, he will crush.
verses.directors_commentary:
Open on the courtroom, not the battlefield. In the ancient Near East the king was the highest judge, and the test of a king was whether the poor could reach him. The people who have no one to speak for them are the first to be named. Play these three verbs as three acts of one will: judge, save, crush. The first two are tender, the third is hard, and the actor should let the voice drop on it.

'Sons of the needy' is an idiom of class, as 'sons of Israel' means Israel: Metzudat David glosses it as the weakest of all, those made frail by poverty and smallness. Do not play it as the beggar's children; the whole class is meant. KJV and ASV keep 'children of the needy', which is literal but can mislead a modern ear into hearing a family line. The last verb, yedakke', is the strong word: 'crush', 'pound to pieces', as Metzudat Zion has it ('breaking and shattering'). KJV's 'break in pieces' is fair. The oppressor ('oshek) is the one who defrauds, and Ibn Ezra defines him as the one who takes a neighbour's wealth by deceit and in secret, so the judge must see what is hidden.

philological_notes.note: 'The afflicted of the people', with the plural construct of 'ani. The root carries the sense of being bowed down, humbled by someone's power, so the word names the poor as the pressed, not only the penniless. Metzudat David adds that the king will give attention to a case even when the sum is small.
An idiom of class: 'sons of the needy' means the needy as a group, here the weakest of them, as Metzudat David reads it.
The oppressor, one who extorts or defrauds. Ibn Ezra stresses the secret, deceitful side of the crime, against open violence (hamas), which he names in v. 14.

verses.translation_literal: They will fear you with [the] sun, and before [the] moon, generation of generations.
verses.translation_dramatic: They will stand in awe of you for as long as the sun climbs and the moon keeps its watch, from one generation to the next, and the next, and the next.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice turns. For three verses the psalm has spoken about the king, and now it speaks to someone as 'you'. Most of the tradition hears God addressed (Rashi, Radak, Meiri): in the king's days the people will learn to fear you. But the shift is abrupt, and some readers, BBE among them, drop the address and give the verse to the king's own long life. Play the line as a prayer breathing out toward heaven, and let the actor decide where the eyes go.

The time words are the sound of eternity in ancient terms: the sun and the moon were the clocks that no one expected to stop. 'With the sun' is 'for as long as the sun'; 'before the moon' is 'while the moon stands before them', as Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Ibn Ezra all explain, 'before' meaning 'in the presence of', in the sense of 'while it lasts'. Ibn Ezra and Meiri compare 'crushed before the moth' (Job 4:19), where 'before' is again temporal or comparative, not spatial; Meiri adds Deuteronomy 7:10 ('to his face'). Modern readers know this as hyperbole, and Radak says so. KJV smooths the two clauses into a single 'as long as the sun and moon endure', which hides that the Hebrew uses two different prepositions for the two lights. The closing 'generation of generations' is a doubled word, a Hebrew way of saying 'always', and KJV's 'throughout all generations' loses the piling-up.

philological_notes.note: 'They will fear you': a second-person suffix on a plural verb. The tradition reads the object as God. BBE and the Septuagint tradition read 'he will continue', which needs a different reading of the consonants. The fear meant here is awe and reverence, not terror.

'Before the moon' means 'in the presence of the moon, as long as it stands', not 'earlier than'. Rashi compares the Mishnaic 'bifnei habayit'. Meiri and Ibn Ezra compare 'lifnei 'ash', 'before the moth' (Job 4:19; Meiri's reference reads 3:9).
A singular followed by its own plural, 'generation of generations': an idiom of unlimited time.

verses.translation_literal: He will come down like rain upon mown grass, like showers, a dripping of the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: He will come down like rain on a field that has just been cut, like the soft showers that soak into the thirsty earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
Every listener in a land that depends on winter rain knows this image. The 'gez' is a pasture freshly mown, the stubble open and thirsty, which springs green at the first rain. Rashi and Metzudat David read the rain as the king's words reaching the people's hearts, and the 'mowing' as the people ready to receive them. Amos 7:1 uses the same noun for the royal mowing of the spring crop (gizzei hamelekh), the king's tax in fodder; so the king here comes to the land that he has taken from.

The KJV 'as showers that water the earth' guesses at zarzif. The word is a hapax legomenon with a stuttering sound (zar-zif); Rashi relates it to the Aramaic and to the Talmud's 'zarzifei demaya', 'drops of water', and Ibn Ezra says it is a four-letter word 'with no equal'. Our literal 'a dripping of the earth' keeps the strangeness. In the Hebrew the verb yered, 'he will come down', is also a royal verb: the king descends from his palace to the gate, as Ibn Ezra notes. Hear the soft consonants: the verse itself drips.

philological_notes.note: 'Fleece / mown grass', from 'to shear'. Radak and Metzudat Zion derive it from the root meaning to cut. Amos 7:1 'the king's mowings' is the same word.
Heavy, fertilising spring showers; the plural of 'rain in many drops'. Metzudat Zion links the root with the archer's shooting (Gen 21:20).
A hapax legomenon, 'dripping', with a quadriliteral root. Rashi and Metzudat Zion cite the Talmudic zarzifei demaya. Ibn Ezra says it has 'no like'.

verses.translation_literal: In his days a righteous one will flourish, and an abundance of peace, until there is no moon.
verses.translation_dramatic: In his days the righteous will blossom, and peace will be heaped up in abundance, until the moon itself is no more.
verses.directors_commentary:
The rain of the last verse has done its work: now the garden blooms. The verb parach is a plant verb, 'to bud, burst into flower', applied here to a person: the righteous 'sprouts'. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak understand 'tzaddiq' as a collective, many righteous. The KJV 'the righteous' is right. 'Rov shalom', 'abundance of peace', is the opposite of the hardscrabble hill-farming of verse 3: more than enough.

The finale is a hyperbole in Eastern court style: 'until there is no moon', Hebrew 'ad bli yareach. The KJV 'so long as the moon endureth' is a smoothed paraphrase of a very stark phrase, 'until not-moon'. Rashi remarks that this prayer was fulfilled except for its endlessness, since Solomon sinned and the kingdom did not last; Radak says on Solomon it is hyperbole, on the Messiah literal. For the actor: the Hebrew imagines an end of the moon and still places peace beyond it.

philological_notes.note: 'He will blossom'. Ibn Ezra links it to the rain of v. 6; Metzudat David glosses it as growing higher and higher.
Literally 'until not-moon'. Metzudat Zion links bli to bliyah, wearing out and ruin. A conventional expression for 'for ever'.

verses.translation_literal: And may he rule from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: May he rule from sea to sea, and from the River out to the very edges of the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The camera pulls back from the plot of grass and the poor man's claim to the whole map. 'The River' is the Euphrates: in Hebrew usage ha-nahar, with no more name, is always that river, the north-east edge of the ideal territory promised to Abraham (Gen 15:18) and in Solomon's day the limit of his sway (1 Kings 5:4, which Rashi cites). 'From sea to sea' is Mediterranean to Red Sea or Dead Sea, depending on the reader (Rashi: from the Red Sea to the sea of the Philistines, citing Exod 23:31).

The KJV 'he shall have dominion also' adds 'also' and 'shall have'; the verb yerd is a jussive and a rare form with a dropped vowel; it comes from radah, 'to tread down', a verb used for the human mandate over the fish in Gen 1:28 (Metzudat Zion). It is a ruler's verb, with a boot in it. And this must be heard with the sound-play of vv. 6 and 8: yered ('he will come down' as rain) and yerd ('he will tread / rule') are nearly identical in sound and spelling. The hearer would catch the echo, and Hebrew poetry intends it: the rain-king and the ruling-king are one person.

philological_notes.note: From radah, 'to rule, tread'. Metzudat Zion compares Gen 1:28. The form sounds like yered, 'he will come down', in v. 6; the sound echo is very likely intended, though it is my own observation.
'The River' is the Euphrates (Targum 'Perat'; Ibn Ezra 'this is the Euphrates'). The Hebrew has no name, a mark of how central the river was.
'The ends of the earth': Metzudat Zion 'extremities'. Ibn Ezra reads it as the wilderness boundary on a geographical reading.

verses.translation_literal: Before him desert-dwellers will bow, and his enemies will lick dust.
verses.translation_dramatic: Before him the people of the dry places will kneel, and his enemies will lick the dust.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the picture is of a court, with the ambassadors arriving. Bowing was the posture of every vassal before every Near Eastern king, and 'licking the dust' is not a figure of speech alone: Assyrian and Egyptian reliefs show captives on their faces in the dirt, and the Amarna letters have vassals writing that they have fallen 'seven times and seven times, on the belly and on the back'. Here that image is lifted into poetry, two lines setting the far nomad against the nearer enemy.

The word tziyim is where translations part. The KJV 'they that dwell in the wilderness' reads it from tziyyah, 'dryness'. But Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion read 'ships' (compare tzi in Num 24:24 and Isa 33:21), which fits the 'islands' of the next verse; Rashi has 'bands (of nobles)'; the Targum 'governors'. The literal layer keeps the oldest reading, 'desert-dwellers'. BBE's 'those who are against him go down before him' drops all of this. Observe, too, that the KJV 'shall lick the dust' is literal and correct.

philological_notes.note: Disputed: 'desert-dwellers' (from tziyyah, drought; Radak 'dwellers in the dry land, such as the Kedarites'), 'ships' (Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David, Metzudat Zion), 'bands' (Rashi, citing Num 24:24). I follow the first.
'They will lick dust': a posture of total submission. Metzudat David reads it as bowing down until the face touches the ground. Metzudat Zion links lachakh to Num 22:4, the ox licking up the grass.

verses.translation_literal: Kings of Tarshish and of the islands will return tribute; kings of Sheba and Seba will bring near a gift.
verses.translation_dramatic: The kings of Tarshish and of the far islands will send their tribute back to him, year after year. The kings of Sheba and of Seba will bring their gifts to his feet.
verses.directors_commentary:
Four names map the known world: Tarshish in the far west, across the sea (probably Tartessos in Spain, or a distant mining port); the 'islands' of the Mediterranean; Sheba, in south Arabia, the land of incense and gold; and Seba, usually placed in Africa beyond Egypt (compare Isa 43:3). Rashi sees the queen of Sheba arriving in 1 Kings 10, and Hiram's Tarshish ships returning every three years with gold and ivory (1 Kings 10:22), the model of this verse.

Here the KJV smooths: 'shall bring presents' for yashivu, which actually means 'will return, pay back'. The ASV and YLT 'render' or 'send back' are closer: tribute is a repeated payment, the verb of coming back again. Radak and Metzudat David explain it that way, as tribute that returns year after year. The second verb is 'bring near' (yaqrivu), the vocabulary of offerings brought near to an altar; and eshkar is a rare word for 'gift' (also Ezek 27:15), used by Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion as a synonym of minchah. The KJV renders them both 'presents / gifts' and loses the shift from paying a debt to making a sacrifice.

philological_notes.note: A causative of 'return': 'they will give back, pay'. Radak and Metzudat David say it was used because the tribute was repeated, comparing 2 Kings 3:4 where Mesha 'returned' a hundred thousand lambs.
A rare word for gift or tribute. Rashi 'a gift'; Ibn Ezra 'like minchah'; Metzudat Zion compares Ezek 27:15 'they returned your 'eshkar'.
A distant sea-trading land; Rashi connects it to the ships of Tarshish in 1 Kings 10:22. Its exact location is uncertain.

verses.translation_literal: And all kings will bow down to him; all nations will serve him.
verses.translation_dramatic: And every king will bend the knee to him, and every nation will take up his service.
verses.directors_commentary:
The two verbs are the grammar of empire. The first, hishtachavah, is full prostration, bowing to the ground, and the second, 'avad, is 'to serve', also 'to work' and 'to worship'. Neither belongs to one use only: both are said of homage paid to kings and of the worship of God. So the Hebrew does not decide between a vassal's courtesy and an act of devotion, and the actor should not decide it either. In the world of Solomon, for a smaller king to bow and bring tribute was the way a treaty was kept.

The messianic reading does not come from these verbs. It comes from the Targum, which opens the psalm with 'for the King Messiah' (Targum on v. 1), and from Radak, who reads the psalm both of Solomon and of the Messiah. KJV's 'Yea' for the plain 'and' is a small padding, and its 'fall down' is sharper than the Hebrew. Ibn Ezra takes the verse as the general statement after the specific kings of Tarshish and Sheba in v. 10: all kings, and the nations under their hand. Malbim adds that the nations will serve willingly, once they have recognised the king's wisdom.

philological_notes.note: 'To bow down, prostrate oneself'. The same verb is used for homage to a king or a superior and for the worship of God, so the verb alone does not say which is meant here.
'They will serve him': 'avad is the ordinary word for service, labour and the service of a master, and also for the worship of God. Here the sense is political subjection.

verses.translation_literal: For he will deliver the needy who cries for help, and the poor, and the one who has no helper.
verses.translation_dramatic: For he will rescue the needy man when he cries out, and the poor, and the one who has no one to help him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The kings and nations of the last verses bow, and this verse says why: not for wealth or fear, but because he rescues the one who cries. 'Ki', 'for', is the hinge; Radak reads it exactly so: they will love and serve him because they will see that he saves the poor.

The cry is the technical language of petition: mesha'ea' (the one who 'cries for help', from the root shava', a cry to a court or to God) is the plaintiff who appeals when he has no patron. A person with 'ein 'ozer, 'no helper', was legally exposed: in ancient Israel a man was protected by a kin-redeemer or a patron, and a poor orphan or widow had none. The king stands in as that missing helper. In the Hebrew 'ozer 'helper' is also one of God's own titles (Ps 33:20; 121:1), so the king is acting in God's role.

The KJV 'when he crieth' turns the participle into a time clause; the Hebrew is more direct, 'the needy, one who cries out', and the second line 'and the poor and no helper to him' has no verb, so the sentence breaks and stumbles, as the poor man does. ASV 'that hath no helper' is a good rendering.

philological_notes.note: 'One crying for help': a participle of the root for a loud appeal for rescue. Metzudat David reads it as 'from the cry he cries because of his oppressors'.
'No helper to him': the person without kin or patron. Metzudat David extends it to everyone with no one to help. The same root forms a title of God.

verses.translation_literal: He will have compassion on [the] poor and needy, and the lives of [the] needy he will save.
verses.translation_dramatic: He will spare the weak. The poor, the destitute, the ones who have nothing: his pity falls on them. And when the needy are fighting for their very breath, it is he who saves them.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play this as the center of the king's job description, not as a nicety. In the ancient Near East a king's duty to protect the dal (the weak, low, 'dangling' person) and the evyon (the one who lacks and begs) was written into royal inscriptions from Mesopotamia to Egypt; a king who failed was understood to rule badly. Notice the double stroke: 'poor and needy' then 'the needy' again. The Hebrew thickens the word to hammer the point, as Radak says: the doubling is for emphasis.

The KJV 'spare' for yachos is fair, but it hides the feeling: the verb is about pity, the look that stops the hand. And KJV 'save the souls' makes a modern ear hear a religious rescue of the afterlife. Nefesh means 'life', the throat, the breathing self; what the king saves is people who are about to die. Malbim hears more, a teaching of conduct, but the plain sense is physical rescue.

philological_notes.note: Not 'souls' in the later sense. The nefesh is the living person, the throat and breath that hunger and cry out. 'Save the lives' is the plain meaning; KJV 'souls' invites a spiritual reading the verse does not need.
To feel compassion, to spare; Metzudat David glosses it as the king being 'protective' of the poor. It is the verb of pity that holds back a blow.

verses.translation_literal: From deceit and from violence he will redeem their life, and their blood will be precious in his eyes.
verses.translation_dramatic: From the quiet fraud and from the raised fist he will buy their lives back. Their blood is dear to him; in his eyes it is costly, not something to be spilled and forgotten.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb is gaal, 'redeem', the vocabulary of the family. The goel is the kinsman who steps in to buy back a relative's land or freedom or to avenge his blood. So the king is being cast as the next of kin of every poor person in the land (Malbim catches this). The actor should feel kinship, not charity.

The pair 'deceit and violence' covers both ways the powerful crush the weak: hidden and open. Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat Zion all read tokh as 'deceit' or a hidden harm, hence 'from deceit', and chamas as the open one. Radak puts it in two lines: deceit without the victim's knowledge, violence with it. The KJV 'deceit and violence' gets this right; the ASV 'oppression' loses the hidden half.

The last line is blunt: 'their blood' is a price word. 'Precious' (yeyakar) means costly, valued, of weight. In an economy where the poor had little else, the king's attention is what gives their lives a price.

philological_notes.note: Usually a separate word from 'midst' (tokh); here the vocalization is read as 'deceit', a related noun of tokh meaning 'oppression, fraud'. Rashi compares Proverbs 29:13 (ish tekhakhim); Metzudat Zion says it names the evil thought hidden within the heart.
Violence and wrongful seizure; the word the flood story uses for what filled the earth. Ibn Ezra reads it as the open form of wrong.
To redeem as a kinsman; the family-duty word. Malbim says the poor are counted as the king's relatives.

verses.translation_literal: And may he live; and [one] will give to him from [the] gold of Sheba, and [one] will pray for him continually; all the day [one] will bless him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Long may he live. Let gold from Sheba be laid at his feet, and let prayer rise for him without ceasing; all the day long let blessing follow him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tone shifts from prediction back to prayer. 'And may he live' (vihi) is a true jussive, a wish: it is the one verb in this verse that grammar marks as a wish. The imperfects that follow can carry on the wish, as BBE reads them ('may gold be given', 'may prayers be made'), or stand as plain futures, as KJV and ASV read them. The Hebrew allows both, and the actor can let the wish slide into confidence. ASV's 'they shall live' is not in the text: the verb is singular.

The verbs have no named subject: 'and [one] will give', 'and [one] will pray', 'and [one] will bless', and this impersonal plural is why KJV builds passives ('shall be given', 'prayer shall be made'), which is fair, but smooths the many hands. Rashi gives God as the giver, citing the promise of wealth and honour to Solomon (1 Kings 3:13). Radak and Meiri read 'may he live' of the poor man, who lives with the king and receives from his gold, and then prays for him; Malbim reads it the same way. 'Gold of Sheba' is a mark of luxury: Sheba, in south Arabia, was the source of gold and incense, and the queen of Sheba brought a hundred and twenty talents to Solomon (1 Kings 10:10). KJV's 'daily shall he be praised' softens 'bless': the Hebrew yevarakhenhu is the word for invoking God's favour on someone, and Rashi observes that a blessing and a prayer are here the same act. 'All the day' is literal, every hour of it.

philological_notes.note: A jussive, 'and may he live': a wish, like the royal acclamation 'yechi hamelekh' ('long live the king'). The verbs after it are ordinary imperfects.
'Gold of Sheba': Sheba is the south-Arabian trading kingdom of gold and spices. Rashi ties the gift to the wealth promised to Solomon.
'May [one] bless him', with a rare extended suffix (-enhu). To bless is to ask God's favour for a person. Rashi says that a prayer and a blessing are the same here.

verses.translation_literal: May there be an abundance of grain in the land, on [the] top of [the] mountains; may its fruit rustle like [the] Lebanon, and may [they] blossom from [the] city like [the] vegetation of the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the land be heavy with grain. Let it stand even on the mountaintops, and let its heads rustle in the wind like the forests of Lebanon. And let the city teem, its people springing up thick as the grass of the field.
verses.directors_commentary:
The picture is of impossible fertility. Grain does not grow on mountaintops, where the soil is thin and the wind is hard, so the wish is for a blessing that overturns the usual limits of the land. In Israel grain grew in the valleys and terraces; everything depended on rain, and the king was thought to hold the rain's favor. A prosperous king means a full harvest.

The word pissat is rare and puzzling: KJV 'handful', ASV 'abundance'. Rashi and Metzudat Zion take it as 'spreading, increase'; Radak and Meiri take it as a handful of seed that grows to fill the hillside. Either way the mountain top is the surprise. 'Rustle like Lebanon' is a sound: wind moving through the cedar forest. The verb yir'ash is also the word for shaking and earthquake, so it is a loud, large sound, not the soft one.

The last clause turns from fields to people. 'Blossom from the city' is the same verb as flowers: the city's people are what blooms. The KJV 'flourish' and its 'they of the city' fill in what the Hebrew leaves bare. Rashi hears Jerusalem, since the Targum says 'from Jerusalem'.

philological_notes.note: A word found only here. Rashi derives it from pasyon, 'spreading, increase'; Metzudat Zion from pasah (Leviticus 13:5); the KJV 'handful' follows Radak and Meiri. Rashi also quotes the Talmud reading of 'cakes' for the Messianic age. Treat the sense as uncertain.
To shake, rattle, quake; used of earthquake and of the roar of armies. Here the swaying heads of grain make a noise like the Lebanon forest in wind.
To blossom, flower; Metzudat Zion compares 'and it blossomed blossoms' (Numbers 17:23). The people of the city are the flowering.

verses.translation_literal: May his name be for ever; before the sun may his name be continued; and may they bless themselves by him; all nations, may they call him fortunate.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let his name last. Let it outlive the dawn, outlast the long road of the sun, and still be spoken when the sun has crossed the sky ten thousand times. Let it pass from father to son and from son to grandson, never going silent. Let the peoples of the earth turn to him when they wish for good. And let every nation, near and far, look at his life and call it blessed.
verses.directors_commentary:
The king's name is the point: in the ancient Near East a name is a person's presence in the world, and a king's name carried in memory, in sons and in royal inscriptions was the nearest thing to immortality. Court language here is the old wish 'may the king live for ever' stretched to the whole span of the sun. 'Before the sun' means 'in the presence of the sun', for as long as it shines, not before it existed. The verb yinnon is rare and the sources split: Radak, Ibn Ezra, Meiri and Malbim hear nin, 'offspring', so the name is handed down like an heir, from son to grandson; Rashi and Metzudat Zion hear a word of rule and lordship, as in Proverbs 29:21. Play both for the actors: a name that is passed on and a name that rules.

Then the line widens to the nations, and here the KJV flattens the Hebrew. 'Men shall be blessed in him' makes the people passive recipients. The verb is a hitpael, 'bless themselves by him': they use his name as the model of blessing, the way Genesis 22:18 and 26:4 promise that all the nations of the earth will bless themselves by Abraham's and Isaac's seed (Genesis 12:3 gives the same promise with the niphal). Rashi and Metzudat David read it as the everyday formula of a father blessing his son: may you be wise and rich like Solomon, may God make you like Solomon. The last verb, ye'asherUhu, is from 'ashar, 'to call fortunate', the root of 'ashrei' ('happy is the man') in Psalm 1:1. KJV 'call him blessed' hides that it is a different word from barak. Nations do not worship him; they point to him as the example of a good life. Because verse 17 is a wish rather than a prediction, the KJV's 'shall' also hardens the mood. Only yehi is a jussive form; the imperfects that follow carry on the wish, as in verse 15, so the whole verse is a prayer for the king.

philological_notes.note: A rare niphal imperfect, read as a wish after yehi. Most read it from nin, 'offspring', hence 'be propagated, sprout': the name continues through heirs, as a son carries the father's name. Rashi and Metzudat Zion instead read a sense of rule or lordship, as in Prov 29:21 manon.

Hitpael of barak: 'and may they bless themselves by him'. The king becomes the standard of the blessing wish. The same stem and idiom appear in Gen 22:18 and 26:4; Gen 12:3 has the niphal variant of the same promise. KJV 'be blessed in him' is the passive reading.
Piel of 'ashar: 'declare fortunate, call happy'. Related to 'ashrei', 'happy is'. Metzudat Zion links it to praise and Radak glosses it as 'they will say: happy is he'.

verses.translation_literal: Blessed [be] YHWH God, [the] God of Israel, [who] does wonders, he alone.
verses.translation_dramatic: Blessed be the LORD God, the God of Israel, who works wonders, and he alone.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice changes: after the king, the singer looks up. This verse and the next are the closing doxology of Book II of the Psalms (compare 41:14, 89:53, 106:48), a liturgical seam the editors placed to mark the end of one scroll-section. Play it as the congregation answering: the loud 'blessed' that follows every long song.

'YHWH God' has two names side by side, which the KJV renders 'the Lord God', with the capitals hiding that the first is the personal name. The key claim is 'who alone does wonders': in a world full of local gods, each credited with its own marvels, the claim is polemical. Radak makes it explicit: the wonders are shown specifically in Israel, so it is the God of Israel and not the gods of the nations who works them. KJV 'only doeth' is archaic, and its word order lets 'only' float. The Hebrew puts 'alone' last, as the punch.

Rashi reads it back into Solomon's reign, tying the wonders to the fire from heaven at the Temple dedication.

philological_notes.note: Wonders, acts that exceed what is expected. Malbim says these are deeds that rise above the natural order, which YHWH does without any natural agent.
'By himself, alone'; the sense is that no other being acts in these wonders. Radak reads it as a contrast with the gods of the nations.

verses.translation_literal: And blessed [be the] name of his glory for ever, and may his glory fill all the earth. Amen and amen.
verses.translation_dramatic: And blessed be his glorious name for ever. May his glory fill the whole earth, from edge to edge. Amen. And amen.
verses.directors_commentary:
The congregation's answer grows. 'The name of his glory' is a Hebrew construction, 'the name of his kavod', where kavod is 'weight', the heaviness of someone important; the KJV 'glorious name' turns the noun into an adjective, which loses the sense of weight. Ibn Ezra and Radak think this is a reference to the unspoken proper name of God.

The second wish, 'may his glory fill all the earth', echoes Numbers 14:21 and Isaiah 6:3, where the seraphim cry that the earth is full of his glory. Radak links it to Isaiah's hope that the earth would be full of the knowledge of the LORD. The verb is a wish, not a statement; the KJV 'let ... be filled' is right.

'Amen and amen' is a seal. The word is from the root of 'faithful, firm'; Metzudat David says the doubling is for strength. It is spoken by the people, not the singer, and the actors should speak it together.

philological_notes.note: 'So be it, it is firm'; from the root of faithfulness. The repetition strengthens it (Metzudat David); Radak reads it as 'may this future thing be fulfilled, true fulfilment'.
From the root 'to be heavy'; glory as weight, importance. English 'glory' hides the physical image.

verses.translation_literal: [They] are finished, the prayers of David, son of Jesse.
verses.translation_dramatic: Here the prayers of David, son of Jesse, come to their end.
verses.directors_commentary:
A line in a different voice: not a prayer but an editor's note, like the words at the foot of a scroll. It closes Book II of the Psalms, and the actor should drop out of the song and into a scribe's flat tone.

The KJV 'are ended' is fine, but the verb kalu also means 'completed' or, with a different shade, 'used up', and the noun tefillot, 'prayers', is the word that gives this collection of Davidic psalms its sense of petition (Radak: not songs or thanksgiving, but prayers for atonement, rescue and success). Radak and Rashi both read it as David's last psalm, spoken as Solomon took the throne.

The statement cannot mean the end of all Davidic psalms, since later books still carry psalms headed 'of David'. Ibn Ezra reports Judah Halevi's view that it is simply the closing mark of a scroll's section, and Rashi says the verse is a note for a collection, not placed in time.

philological_notes.note: 'They are finished, completed'. Rashi offers two readings: a rabbinic one that makes 'kalu' mean 'all of these', and 'nistayyemu' (they are concluded), comparing the verb in Job 24:24. Ibn Ezra rejects the 'all' reading.
Prayers, petitions. Radak stresses the word choice: 'prayers' and not 'songs', because they ask for atonement and rescue.
